title: Review the AI Slide Outline First: A Public PDF Becomes 4 Slides with Sources
description:
What must an outline decide before a public PDF becomes a four-slide presentation?
For everyday workers who need to deliver slides that can be edited and traced to their sources.

This original local example was completed on 2026-10-25. The author's brief, two-page draft, consolidated feedback and revision stages were saved in one generation run. They are not Notebook product responses or a real interactive review pause. Google's 2026-10-19 announcement provides workflow context; I did not sign in to or test the product.

The data are 2025 statistics in the economics chapter of Stanford's 2026 AI Index. Amounts follow Quid's investment scope: the corporate total includes the private subset, so do not add them. Regional comparisons cover private AI investment only. The 88% figure is the share of respondents who report that their organization uses AI in at least one business function. Whether the questions and denominators behind 70% and 79% align remains unresolved; both stay in notes.

In the citation list, slide 1 is the author's overview of the questions; slides 2–4 identify locations in the original report.

The delivered PDF consists of page images. The PPTX retains native text and shapes. It was reopened to inspect its structure, but has not been rendered natively in PowerPoint.

Full reusable prompt:
Use only this public PDF I provide to make four slides for coworkers. Aim for about three minutes. Give me the outline first; do not generate slides yet.
Answer one question per slide. List the figures, data year and units to use. List the survey population or statistical scope, printed report page numbers and PDF page positions. Separate investment amounts from usage percentages. Do not add a total to one of its subsets.
If sources do not align, mark the issue for confirmation; do not pick a figure for me. Wait for my single batch of feedback before producing the four slides. Also deliver an editable file, a PDF and a slide-by-slide citation list. Keep unconfirmed figures in notes; do not chart them as settled conclusions.
